notes.front: What is an amplifier’s operating point?
notes.back: The steady (quiescent) condition of the amplifying device with no signal applied, set by its bias.
notes.explanation: Where the operating point sits decides for how much of the input cycle output current flows, and so the class of operation.
notes.example: Like where a see-saw rests before anyone pushes: every swing of the signal is measured from there.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 8, chapter 1, classes of operation, p. 1-6
notes.evidence: This is a function of the operating point of the amplifying device. The operating point of the amplifying device is determined by the bias applied to the device.

notes.front: What is a common-emitter amplifier?
notes.back: The transistor configuration with the emitter common to input and output; the most used arrangement, giving good voltage, current and power gain.
notes.explanation: The input is applied between base and emitter; it is also the only configuration whose output is phase-reversed.
notes.example: Like the workhorse lorry of a fleet: not specialised, but good all round, so it is used most.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 7, chapter 2, common emitter, p. 2-24
notes.evidence: is the arrangement most frequently used in practical amplifier circuits, since it provides good voltage, current, and power gain.

notes.front: What is a common-collector amplifier?
notes.back: A transistor amplifier with the input on the base, the output from the emitter, and the collector common to both.
notes.explanation: The Navy course likens it to the vacuum-tube cathode follower: both have high input and low output resistance.
notes.example: Like a porter who takes a heavy case from a frail sender and carries it at full strength to the recipient.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 7, chapter 2, common collector, p. 2-27
notes.evidence: In the common-collector circuit, the input signal is applied to the base, the output is taken from the emitter, and the collector is the element common to both input and output.

notes.front: What is an emitter follower?
notes.back: Another name for the common-collector amplifier: high input impedance and low output impedance.
notes.explanation: Its output is taken from the emitter, with the collector common to input and output.
notes.example: Like a stage placed after a high-impedance crystal microphone so that it can drive a long, low-impedance cable.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 8, chapter 1, summary, p. 1-36
notes.evidence: The COMMON-COLLECTOR (EMITTER FOLLOWER) configuration of a transistor amplifier as HIGH INPUT and LOW OUTPUT IMPEDANCE.

notes.front: What is voltage divider bias?
notes.back: Base bias taken from a pair of resistors across the supply, forming a voltage divider; the most widely used combination-bias system.
notes.explanation: The divider holds the base bias steady while an emitter resistor adds self-bias, which improves thermal stability.
notes.example: Like tapping a fixed fraction of a tank’s pressure off a pair of valves to set a gauge.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 7, chapter 2, combination bias, p. 2-20
notes.evidence: One of the most widely used combination-bias systems is the voltage-divider type shown in figure 2-14.

notes.front: What is self bias in a transistor amplifier?
notes.back: Bias the transistor develops from its own current, for example across a resistor in series with the emitter, opposing changes in that current.
notes.explanation: If emitter current rises, the drop across the emitter resistor rises too and pushes back against the change.
notes.example: Like a car that eases its own throttle when it speeds up downhill.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 7, chapter 2, combination bias, p. 2-20
notes.evidence: Resistor R3, which is connected in series with the emitter, provides the emitter with self-bias. Should IE increase, the voltage drop across R3 would also increase

notes.front: What is a push-pull amplifier?
notes.back: A single stage with two transistors driven 180° out of phase, whose outputs are combined.
notes.explanation: Combining the two outputs gives more gain than one transistor could supply alone.
notes.example: Like two people on a two-handled saw, one pulling while the other pushes.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 8, chapter 1, push-pull amplifiers, p. 1-29
notes.evidence: These transistors are configured in such a way that the two outputs, 180º out of phase with each other, combine. This allows more gain than one transistor could supply by itself.

notes.front: What is a Class D amplifier?
notes.back: An amplifier that uses switching technology to achieve high efficiency.
notes.explanation: Its devices switch rather than operating in their linear region.
notes.example: Like controlling a lamp’s brightness by flicking it on and off very fast rather than with a dimmer that runs warm.
notes.evidence: An amplifier that uses switching technology to achieve high efficiency

notes.front: What is a parasitic suppressor?
notes.back: A component fitted to an RF power amplifier to prevent unwanted oscillations.
notes.explanation: The pool offers it, with neutralizing the stage, as the way to stop unwanted oscillation in an RF power amplifier.
notes.example: Like a ferrite bead slipped over a transistor HF amplifier’s input and output leads to damp VHF and UHF oscillation.
notes.evidence: What can be done to prevent unwanted oscillations in an RF power amplifier? A. Tune the stage for minimum loading B. Tune both the input and output for maximum power C. Install parasitic suppressors and/or neutralize the stage

notes.front: What is a grounded-grid amplifier, and what input impedance does it have?
notes.back: A vacuum tube amplifier with its control grid at ground; it has a low input impedance.
notes.explanation: The pool gives low input impedance as its characteristic, rather than high power gain.
notes.example: Like a transistor common-base stage, with the grid in the place of the base and the drive fed to the cathode.
notes.evidence: What is a characteristic of a grounded-grid amplifier? A. High power gain B. Low input impedance

notes.front: What is a differential amplifier?
notes.back: An amplifier that can have two inputs and/or two outputs, and amplifies the difference between two input signals.
notes.explanation: It will also cancel out signals that are common to its two inputs.
notes.example: Like a balance scale: it responds only to the difference between the two pans, not their shared weight.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 8, chapter 3, differential amplifiers, p. 3-2
notes.evidence: A differential amplifier is an amplifier that can have two input signals and/or two output signals. This amplifier can amplify the difference between two input signals.

notes.front: What is an inverting amplifier?
notes.back: An op-amp circuit whose input and feedback resistor both go to the inverting input; its output is 180° out of phase with the input.
notes.explanation: Feedback from the output holds the inverting input very close to 0 volts, a virtual ground, when the non-inverting input is grounded.
notes.example: Like a see-saw: push one end up and the other goes down by an amount set by where the pivot sits.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 8, chapter 3, inverting configuration, p. 3-19
notes.evidence: As you can see in figure 3-13, the output signal is 180 degrees out of phase with the input signal.

notes.front: What is an op-amp’s input offset voltage?
notes.back: The differential input voltage needed to bring the open-loop output voltage to zero.
notes.explanation: The pool defines it by the open-loop output: it is the input difference that brings that output to zero.
notes.example: Like the small weight you add to one pan to make a slightly unequal balance read level.
notes.evidence: The differential input voltage needed to bring the open loop output voltage to zero

notes.front: What is an op-amp’s gain-bandwidth product?
notes.back: Gain multiplied by bandwidth: the same for every circuit built with that op-amp, and equal to the unity-gain frequency.
notes.explanation: Lowering a circuit’s gain with feedback widens its bandwidth, and the product stays fixed.
notes.example: Like a fixed length of rope: make the loop taller (more gain) and it must get narrower (less bandwidth).
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 8, chapter 3, bandwidth, p. 3-28
notes.evidence: The relationship between circuit gain and bandwidth in an operational-amplifier circuit can be expressed by the GAIN-BANDWIDTH PRODUCT (GAIN × BANDWIDTH = UNITY GAIN POINT).

notes.front: What prevents unwanted ringing and audio instability in an op-amp audio filter?
notes.back: Restricting both the gain and the Q.
notes.explanation: A high-Q filter keeps sounding after the signal stops, and high gain pushes the circuit towards oscillation, so keeping both modest keeps it stable.
notes.example: Like a wine glass that keeps sounding after it has been tapped.
notes.evidence: How can unwanted ringing and audio instability be prevented in an op-amp audio filter? A. Restrict both gain and Q

notes.front: For what part of the input signal does a Class A amplifier conduct?
notes.back: All of it: 100 percent, or 360°.
notes.explanation: The output is a full copy of the input, which gives Class A good fidelity and low efficiency.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 8, chapter 1, class A operation, p. 1-6
notes.evidence: Since the output signal is a 100% (or 360º) copy of the input signal, current in the output circuit must flow for 100% of the input signal time.

notes.front: For what share of the input signal does current flow in a Class AB amplifier?
notes.back: 51 to 99 percent: more than half the cycle but less than all of it.
notes.explanation: The Navy course defines Class AB by this bias range, between Class B’s 50 percent and Class A’s 100 percent.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 8, chapter 1, class AB operation, p. 1-7
notes.evidence: If the amplifying device is biased in such a way that current flows in the device for 51% - 99% of the input signal, the amplifier is operating class AB.

notes.front: What are Class C’s efficiency and fidelity like?
notes.back: It is the most efficient class but has the worst fidelity.
notes.explanation: The device conducts for only a small portion of the input signal, so the output bears little resemblance to the input.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 8, chapter 1, class C operation, p. 1-8
notes.evidence: Since the transistor does not conduct except during a small portion of the input signal, this is the most efficient amplifier. It also has the worst fidelity.

notes.front: Where does the Navy course say push-pull amplifiers are used?
notes.back: Where high power output and good fidelity are needed, such as receiver output stages, public address amplifiers and amplitude modulators.
notes.explanation: The course’s example circuit runs Class A, but it notes that Class AB or Class B operation can be used.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 8, chapter 1, push-pull amplifiers, p. 1-29
notes.evidence: This "push-pull" amplifier is used where high power output and good fidelity are needed: receiver output stages, public address amplifiers, and AM modulators, for example.

notes.front: Which transistor configuration reverses the phase of the signal?
notes.back: The common emitter, the only one of the three that does.
notes.explanation: In common-base and common-collector stages, output and input stay in phase.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 7, chapter 2, common emitter, p. 2-25
notes.evidence: The common-emitter circuit is the only configuration that provides a phase reversal.

notes.front: What is the common-collector configuration mostly used for?
notes.back: Impedance matching; it is also used as a current driver because of its substantial current gain.
notes.explanation: Like the vacuum-tube cathode follower, it has high input and low output resistance.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 7, chapter 2, common collector, p. 2-27
notes.evidence: The common-collector configuration (CC) shown in figure 2-16 view C is used mostly for impedance matching. It is also used as a current driver, because of its substantial current gain.

notes.front: Why is a bypass capacitor placed across the emitter resistor of a combination-biased amplifier?
notes.back: To keep the resistor’s long-term thermal stability while allowing little signal degeneration.
notes.explanation: A large enough capacitor does not change its charge with rapid signal variations, so the signal is not degenerated.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 7, chapter 2, combination bias, p. 2-20
notes.evidence: to provide long-term or dc thermal stability, and at the same time, allow minimal ac signal degeneration, the bypass capacitor (Cbp) is placed across R3.

notes.front: What are the three most important characteristics of an operational amplifier?
notes.back: Very high gain; very high input impedance; very low output impedance.
notes.explanation: No single stage provides all three well enough, so an op-amp chains several stages together.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 8, chapter 3, operational amplifiers, p. 3-16
notes.evidence: 1. Very high gain 2. Very high input impedance 3. Very low output impedance

notes.front: What does degenerative feedback do to the bandwidth of an op-amp circuit?
notes.back: It increases it.
notes.explanation: Feedback lowers the circuit gain, and with the gain-bandwidth product fixed, the bandwidth rises.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 8, chapter 3, bandwidth, p. 3-26
notes.evidence: The use of degenerative feedback increases the bandwidth of an operational amplifier circuit.

notes.front: In an inverting op-amp circuit, what sets the gain?
notes.back: The ratio of the feedback resistor to the input resistor.
notes.explanation: Swapping the feedback resistor for a larger one raises the gain in proportion.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 8, chapter 3, summing amplifier, p. 3-32
notes.evidence: The gain of the circuit is determined by the ratio between the feedback resistor and the input resistors.

notes.front: An amplifier’s bias lets current flow for about 70 percent of each input cycle. Which class is it?
notes.choices:
A) Class AB
B) Class A
C) Class B
D) Class C
notes.back: Class AB
notes.choicesExplained: B: Class A conducts for the whole cycle. C: Class B conducts for 50 percent. D: Class C conducts for less than half the cycle.
notes.explanation: Anything from 51 to 99 percent of the cycle is Class AB.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 8, chapter 1, class AB operation, p. 1-7
notes.evidence: If the amplifying device is biased in such a way that current flows in the device for 51% - 99% of the input signal, the amplifier is operating class AB.

notes.front: A high-impedance audio source must drive a low-impedance load without loading the source. Which transistor stage suits best?
notes.choices:
A) An emitter follower
B) A grounded-grid amplifier
C) A Class C amplifier
D) A common base stage
notes.back: An emitter follower
notes.choicesExplained: B: a grounded-grid amplifier has a low input impedance, which would load the source. C: Class C distorts the signal badly. D: a common-base stage has a low input resistance, so it too would load the source.
notes.explanation: Its high input and low output impedance make it the configuration used mostly for impedance matching.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 7, chapter 2, common collector, p. 2-27
notes.evidence: is used mostly for impedance matching. It is also used as a current driver, because of its substantial current gain.

notes.front: An op-amp has a gain-bandwidth product of 3 MHz. About what bandwidth does a circuit with a gain of 30 have?
notes.choices:
A) 100 kHz
B) 90 MHz
C) 3 MHz
D) 10 kHz
notes.back: 100 kHz
notes.choicesExplained: B: multiplies instead of dividing. C: that is the bandwidth at a gain of one. D: that would be the bandwidth at a gain of 300.
notes.explanation: Gain times bandwidth stays constant, so bandwidth = 3 MHz ÷ 30.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 8, chapter 3, bandwidth, p. 3-28
notes.evidence: the gain times the bandwidth for one configuration of an operational amplifier will equal the gain times the bandwidth for any other configuration of the same operational amplifier.

notes.front: In Figure E7-3, R1 is 2,000 ohms, RF is 20,000 ohms and +0.5 volts DC is applied to the input. What is the output voltage?
notes.choices:
A) −5 volts
B) +5 volts
C) −0.05 volts
D) +10 volts
notes.back: −5 volts
notes.choicesExplained: B: forgets that the inverting circuit reverses the sign. C: divides by the gain instead of multiplying. D: gives twice the correct size with the wrong sign.
notes.explanation: The gain is RF ÷ R1 = 10, and the inverting circuit reverses the sign: 0.5 × −10 = −5 volts.

image.alt: Figure E7-3: an op-amp circuit. The input passes through resistor R1 to the op-amp’s inverting (−) input. Feedback resistor RF runs from the output back to that same input. The non-inverting (+) input is grounded, and the output is taken between the op-amp output and ground.
image.credit: NCVEC Question Pool Committee, 2024–2028 Extra Pool, figure E7-3

notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 8, chapter 3, summing amplifier, p. 3-32
notes.evidence: The gain of the circuit is determined by the ratio between the feedback resistor and the input resistors.

notes.front: What absolute voltage gain does Figure E7-3 give with R1 at 1,000 ohms and RF at 22,000 ohms?
notes.choicesExplained: B: divides R1 by RF, upside down. C: adds one, which is the non-inverting formula. D: slips a decimal place.
notes.explanation: The feedback-to-input resistor ratio sets the gain: 22,000 ÷ 1,000 = 22.

image.alt: Figure E7-3: an op-amp circuit. The input passes through resistor R1 to the op-amp’s inverting (−) input. Feedback resistor RF runs from the output back to that same input. The non-inverting (+) input is grounded, and the output is taken between the op-amp output and ground.
image.credit: NCVEC Question Pool Committee, 2024–2028 Extra Pool, figure E7-3

notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 8, chapter 3, summing amplifier, p. 3-32
notes.evidence: The gain of the circuit is determined by the ratio between the feedback resistor and the input resistors.

notes.front: In Figure E7-1, what does C3 do?
notes.choices:
A) Emitter bypass
B) Input coupling
C) Output coupling
D) Voltage divider bias
notes.back: Emitter bypass
notes.choicesExplained: B: C1 couples the input. C: C2 couples the output. D: R1 and R2 form the divider.
notes.explanation: C3 sits across the emitter resistor R3, keeping its thermal stability while letting the signal pass with little degeneration.

image.alt: Figure E7-1: a transistor amplifier. The input passes through capacitor C1 to the transistor’s base. Resistor R1 runs from the base to the positive supply and R2 from the base to ground. A resistor from the positive supply feeds the collector, and capacitor C2 couples the collector to the output. Resistor R3 runs from the emitter to ground, with capacitor C3 also from the emitter to ground.
image.credit: NCVEC Question Pool Committee, 2024–2028 Extra Pool, figure E7-1

notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 7, chapter 2, combination bias, p. 2-20
notes.evidence: to provide long-term or dc thermal stability, and at the same time, allow minimal ac signal degeneration, the bypass capacitor (Cbp) is placed across R3.

notes.front: A transistor stage’s output is in phase with its input, with high input and low output impedance. Which configuration is it?
notes.choices:
A) Common collector
B) Common emitter
C) Grounded-grid amplifier
D) Differential amplifier
notes.back: Common collector
notes.choicesExplained: B: the common emitter reverses the phase. C: a grounded-grid amplifier has low input impedance. D: a differential amplifier takes two inputs.
notes.explanation: Only the common emitter reverses phase, and high input with low output impedance marks the emitter follower.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 8, chapter 1, summary, p. 1-36
notes.evidence: The COMMON-COLLECTOR (EMITTER FOLLOWER) configuration of a transistor amplifier as HIGH INPUT and LOW OUTPUT IMPEDANCE.

notes.front: How do Class A and Class C amplifiers compare on fidelity and efficiency?
notes.back: Class A: good fidelity, low efficiency. Class C: most efficient, worst fidelity.
notes.explanation: Conduction time trades one for the other: Class A conducts all cycle, Class C only a small part of it.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 8, chapter 1, class A operation, p. 1-6
notes.evidence: The class A amplifier has the characteristics of good FIDELITY and low EFFICIENCY.

notes.front: In a combination-biased amplifier, how do the divider resistors and the emitter resistor differ in what they do?
notes.back: The divider resistors hold the base bias constant; the emitter resistor’s bias changes with emitter current.
notes.explanation: Together they greatly improve thermal stability while keeping the correct operating point.
notes.source: US Navy NEETS Module 7, chapter 2, combination bias, p. 2-20
notes.evidence: the fixed-bias resistors, R1 and R2, tend to keep the base bias constant while the emitter bias changes with emitter conduction. This action greatly improves thermal stability

notes.front: How does an ideal op-amp’s gain differ from a real op-amp circuit’s gain as frequency rises?
notes.back: An ideal op-amp’s gain does not vary with frequency; a real circuit’s gain falls, to one at its unity-gain frequency.
notes.explanation: The real circuit trades gain for bandwidth, fixed by its gain-bandwidth product.
notes.evidence: How does the gain of an ideal operational amplifier vary with frequency? A. It increases linearly with increasing frequency B. It decreases linearly with increasing frequency C. It decreases logarithmically with increasing frequency D. It does not vary with frequency

notes.front: For what portion of the signal cycle does each active element in a push-pull, Class AB amplifier conduct?
notes.choices:
A) More than 180 degrees but less than 360 degrees
B) Exactly 180 degrees
C) The entire cycle
D) Less than 180 degrees
notes.back: More than 180 degrees but less than 360 degrees
notes.choicesExplained: B: exactly 180° is Class B. C: the entire cycle is Class A. D: less than 180° is Class C.
notes.explanation: Class AB conducts for more than half the cycle but less than all of it, so each push-pull device covers over 180°.
notes.evidence: For what portion of the signal cycle does each active element in a push-pull, Class AB amplifier conduct?

notes.front: What is a Class D amplifier?
notes.choices:
A) An amplifier that uses switching technology to achieve high efficiency
B) A low power amplifier that uses a differential amplifier for improved linearity
C) An amplifier that uses drift-mode FETs for high efficiency
D) An amplifier biased to be relatively free from distortion
notes.back: An amplifier that uses switching technology to achieve high efficiency
notes.choicesExplained: B: a differential amplifier for linearity is not the definition. C: drift-mode FETs are not what defines it. D: bias for low distortion describes Class A.
notes.explanation: Its devices switch rather than amplify linearly, which is where the efficiency comes from.
notes.evidence: What is a Class D amplifier?

notes.front: What circuit is required at the output of an RF switching amplifier?
notes.choices:
A) A filter to remove harmonic content
B) A high-pass filter to compensate for low gain at low frequencies
C) A matched load resistor to prevent damage by switching transients
D) A temperature compensating load resistor to improve linearity
notes.back: A filter to remove harmonic content
notes.choicesExplained: B: low-frequency gain is not the issue. C and D: load resistors neither remove harmonics nor are required.
notes.explanation: A switching amplifier’s on-off output is close to a square wave, which is rich in harmonics, so a filter must remove them before the signal reaches the antenna.
notes.evidence: What circuit is required at the output of an RF switching amplifier?

notes.front: What is the operating point of a Class A common emitter amplifier?
notes.choices:
A) Approximately halfway between saturation and cutoff
B) Approximately halfway between the emitter voltage and the base voltage
C) At a point where the bias resistor equals the load resistor
D) At a point where the load line intersects the zero bias current curve
notes.back: Approximately halfway between saturation and cutoff
notes.choicesExplained: B: emitter and base voltages are not the limits of the swing. C: equal bias and load resistors do not define it. D: zero bias current would be cutoff.
notes.explanation: Sitting halfway between saturation and cutoff lets the signal swing equally either way without reaching either limit, so current flows for the whole cycle, as Class A requires.
notes.evidence: What is the operating point of a Class A common emitter amplifier?

notes.front: What can be done to prevent unwanted oscillations in an RF power amplifier?
notes.choices:
A) Tune the stage for minimum loading
B) Tune both the input and output for maximum power
C) Install parasitic suppressors and/or neutralize the stage
D) Use a phase inverter in the output filter
notes.back: Install parasitic suppressors and/or neutralize the stage
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: tuning for loading or maximum power does not stop oscillation. D: a phase inverter in the output filter is not a cure.
notes.explanation: Oscillation needs feedback: neutralising the stage cancels the feedback through the device’s internal capacitance, and parasitic suppressors damp oscillation at frequencies far above the working one.
notes.evidence: What can be done to prevent unwanted oscillations in an RF power amplifier?

notes.front: What is a characteristic of a grounded-grid amplifier?
notes.choices:
A) High power gain
B) Low input impedance
C) High electrostatic damage protection
D) Low bandwidth
notes.back: Low input impedance
notes.choicesExplained: A: high power gain is not its characteristic. C: electrostatic protection is unrelated. D: low bandwidth is not the characteristic either.
notes.explanation: With the grid grounded, the drive goes into the cathode, which carries the tube’s whole current, so the input draws current and looks like a low impedance, as a transistor common-base stage does.
notes.evidence: What is a characteristic of a grounded-grid amplifier?

notes.front: Which of the following is the likely result of using a Class C amplifier to amplify a single-sideband phone signal?
notes.choices:
A) Reduced intermodulation products
B) Increased overall intelligibility
C) Reduced third-order intermodulation
D) Signal distortion and excessive bandwidth
notes.back: Signal distortion and excessive bandwidth
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: a nonlinear amplifier increases intermodulation. B: distortion lowers intelligibility.
notes.explanation: Class C conducts for only a small part of the cycle, so its output bears little resemblance to its input: an SSB signal comes out distorted and wide.
notes.evidence: Which of the following is the likely result of using a Class C amplifier to amplify a single-sideband phone signal?

notes.front: Why are switching amplifiers more efficient than linear amplifiers?
notes.choices:
A) Switching amplifiers operate at higher voltages
B) The switching device is at saturation or cutoff most of the time
C) Linear amplifiers have high gain resulting in higher harmonic content
D) Switching amplifiers use push-pull circuits
notes.back: The switching device is at saturation or cutoff most of the time
notes.choicesExplained: A: higher voltage is not the reason. C: harmonic content is not about efficiency. D: push-pull is used by linear amplifiers too.
notes.explanation: At saturation the device has almost no voltage across it and at cutoff almost no current through it, so little power is wasted as heat in either state.
notes.evidence: Why are switching amplifiers more efficient than linear amplifiers?

notes.front: What is characteristic of an emitter follower (or common collector) amplifier?
notes.choices:
A) Low input impedance and phase inversion from input to output
B) Differential inputs and single output
C) Acts as an OR circuit if one input is grounded
D) Input and output signals in-phase
notes.back: Input and output signals in-phase
notes.choicesExplained: A: it has high input impedance and no phase inversion. B: differential inputs belong to a differential amplifier. C: it is not a logic gate.
notes.explanation: Only the common-emitter configuration reverses phase, so an emitter follower’s output stays in phase with its input.
notes.evidence: What is characteristic of an emitter follower (or common collector) amplifier?

notes.front: In Figure E7-1, what is the purpose of R1 and R2?
notes.choices:
A) Load resistors
B) Voltage divider bias
C) Self bias
D) Feedback
notes.back: Voltage divider bias
notes.choicesExplained: A: the collector resistor is the load. C: self bias comes from the emitter resistor, R3. D: R1 and R2 do not feed output back to input.
notes.explanation: R1 and R2 form a voltage divider from the supply that holds the base bias steady.
notes.evidence: In Figure E7-1, what is the purpose of R1 and R2?

A resistor from the positive supply feeds the collector, and capacitor C2 couples the collector to the output. Resistor R3 runs from the emitter to ground, with capacitor C3 also from the emitter to ground.

notes.front: In Figure E7-1, what is the purpose of R3?
notes.choices:
A) Fixed bias
B) Emitter bypass
C) Output load resistor
D) Self bias
notes.back: Self bias
notes.choicesExplained: A: fixed bias comes from the divider, R1 and R2. B: the emitter bypass is capacitor C3. C: the output load is the collector resistor.
notes.explanation: R3 in series with the emitter provides self bias: more emitter current means more drop across it, opposing the change.
notes.evidence: In Figure E7-1, what is the purpose of R3?

image.alt: Figure E7-1: a transistor amplifier. The input passes through capacitor C1 to the transistor’s base. Resistor R1 runs from the base to the positive supply and R2 from the base to ground. A resistor from the positive supply feeds the collector, and capacitor C2 couples the collector to the output. Resistor R3 runs from the emitter to ground, with capacitor C3 also from the emitter to ground.
image.credit: NCVEC Question Pool Committee, 2024–2028 Extra Pool, figure E7-1

notes.front: What type of amplifier circuit is shown in Figure E7-1?
notes.choices:
A) Common base
B) Common collector
C) Common emitter
D) Emitter follower
notes.back: Common emitter
notes.choicesExplained: A: in common base the input would go to the emitter. B and D: in common collector the output would come from the emitter.
notes.explanation: The input goes to the base, the output comes from the collector, and the emitter is bypassed to ground, so the emitter is common to both.
notes.evidence: What type of amplifier circuit is shown in Figure E7-1?

image.alt: Figure E7-1: a transistor amplifier. The input passes through capacitor C1 to the transistor’s base. Resistor R1 runs from the base to the positive supply and R2 from the base to ground. A resistor from the positive supply feeds the collector, and capacitor C2 couples the collector to the output. Resistor R3 runs from the emitter to ground, with capacitor C3 also from the emitter to ground.

notes.front: What is the typical output impedance of an op-amp?
notes.choices:
A) Very low
B) Very high
C) 100 ohms
D) 10,000 ohms
notes.back: Very low
notes.choicesExplained: B: very high is its input impedance. C and D: fixed values such as 100 or 10,000 ohms are not typical.
notes.explanation: Very low output impedance is one of the three defining characteristics of an operational amplifier.
notes.evidence: What is the typical output impedance of an op-amp?

notes.front: What is the frequency response of the circuit in E7-3 if a capacitor is added across the feedback resistor?
notes.choices:
A) High-pass filter
B) Low-pass filter
C) Band-pass filter
D) Notch filter
notes.back: Low-pass filter
notes.choicesExplained: A: high frequencies are cut, not passed. C and D: a single capacitor across RF gives neither a band-pass nor a notch response.
notes.explanation: A capacitor across RF lowers the feedback impedance as frequency rises, so the gain falls at high frequencies.
notes.evidence: What is the frequency response of the circuit in E7-3 if a capacitor is added across the feedback resistor?

notes.front: What is the typical input impedance of an op-amp?
notes.choices:
A) 100 ohms
B) 10,000 ohms
C) Very low
D) Very high
notes.back: Very high
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: fixed values of 100 or 10,000 ohms are not typical. C: very low is its output impedance.
notes.explanation: Very high input impedance is one of the three defining characteristics of an operational amplifier.
notes.evidence: What is the typical input impedance of an op-amp?

notes.front: What is meant by the term “op-amp input offset voltage”?
notes.choices:
A) The output voltage of the op-amp minus its input voltage
B) The difference between the output voltage of the op-amp and the input voltage required in the immediately following stage
C) The differential input voltage needed to bring the open loop output voltage to zero
D) The potential between the amplifier input terminals of the op-amp in an open loop condition
notes.back: The differential input voltage needed to bring the open loop output voltage to zero
notes.choicesExplained: A and B: output minus input voltages are not offsets. D: the potential between the inputs in open loop is not the definition.
notes.explanation: It is the small input difference needed to null the output with no feedback applied.
notes.evidence: What is meant by the term “op-amp input offset voltage”?

notes.front: How can unwanted ringing and audio instability be prevented in an op-amp audio filter?
notes.choices:
A) Restrict both gain and Q
B) Restrict gain but increase Q
C) Restrict Q but increase gain
D) Increase both gain and Q
notes.back: Restrict both gain and Q
notes.choicesExplained: B, C and D: raising either gain or Q works against stability.
notes.explanation: High Q makes a filter slow to die away after a signal, which is ringing, and high gain brings it close to oscillating; restricting both removes the two causes.
notes.evidence: How can unwanted ringing and audio instability be prevented in an op-amp audio filter?

notes.front: What is the gain-bandwidth of an operational amplifier?
notes.choices:
A) The maximum frequency for a filter circuit using that type of amplifier
B) The frequency at which the open-loop gain of the amplifier equals one
C) The gain of the amplifier at a filter’s cutoff frequency
D) The frequency at which the amplifier’s offset voltage is zero
notes.back: The frequency at which the open-loop gain of the amplifier equals one
notes.choicesExplained: A: it is not a filter frequency limit. C: gain at a cutoff frequency is not the definition. D: offset voltage is unrelated.
notes.explanation: Gain times bandwidth is constant, so it equals the frequency at which the gain has fallen to one.
notes.evidence: What is the gain-bandwidth of an operational amplifier?

notes.front: What voltage gain can be expected from the circuit in Figure E7-3 when R1 is 10 ohms and RF is 470 ohms?
notes.choicesExplained: A: a gain below one would mean the circuit attenuates; even the ratio upside down, 10 ÷ 470, is about 0.02. B: multiplies the resistors. D: halves the correct answer.
notes.explanation: Dividing the feedback resistor by the input resistor gives the gain: 470 ÷ 10.
notes.evidence: What voltage gain can be expected from the circuit in Figure E7-3 when R1 is 10 ohms and RF is 470 ohms?

notes.front: How does the gain of an ideal operational amplifier vary with frequency?
notes.choices:
A) It increases linearly with increasing frequency
B) It decreases linearly with increasing frequency
C) It decreases logarithmically with increasing frequency
D) It does not vary with frequency
notes.back: It does not vary with frequency
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C: each describes a gain that changes with frequency, which the ideal does not.
notes.explanation: An ideal op-amp is a model with no frequency limits; a real one’s gain falls with frequency.
notes.evidence: How does the gain of an ideal operational amplifier vary with frequency?

notes.front: What will be the output voltage of the circuit shown in Figure E7-3 if R1 is 1,000 ohms, RF is 10,000 ohms, and 0.23 volts DC is applied to the input?
notes.choices:
A) 0.23 volts
B) 2.3 volts
C) -0.23 volts
D) -2.3 volts
notes.back: -2.3 volts
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: ignore the gain. B: has the right size but misses the inversion.
notes.explanation: Gain is 10,000 ÷ 1,000 = 10 and the circuit inverts: 0.23 × −10 = −2.3 volts.
notes.evidence: What will be the output voltage of the circuit shown in Figure E7-3 if R1 is 1,000 ohms, RF is 10,000 ohms, and 0.23 volts DC is applied to the input?

notes.front: What absolute voltage gain can be expected from the circuit in Figure E7-3 when R1 is 1,800 ohms and RF is 68 kilohms?
notes.choicesExplained: A: the circuit clearly has gain. B: divides R1 by RF. D: doubles the correct answer.
notes.explanation: Gain is 68,000 ÷ 1,800, which is about 38.

notes.front: What is an operational amplifier?
notes.choices:
A) A high-gain, direct-coupled differential amplifier with very high input impedance and very low output impedance
B) A digital audio amplifier whose characteristics are determined by components external to the amplifier
C) An amplifier used to increase the average output of frequency modulated amateur signals to the legal limit
D) A RF amplifier used in the UHF and microwave regions
notes.back: A high-gain, direct-coupled differential amplifier with very high input impedance and very low output impedance
notes.choicesExplained: B: it is an analog, not a digital, amplifier. C: it has nothing to do with FM power limits. D: it is not an RF power amplifier for UHF and microwaves.
notes.explanation: It is a direct-coupled, high-gain differential amplifier whose defining traits include very high input and very low output impedance.
notes.evidence: What is an operational amplifier?
